'''''Thuja occidentalis''''', also known as '''northern white-cedar''',{{r|iucn}} '''eastern white-cedar''',{{r|vascan}} or '''eastern arborvitae''',{{r|vascan|GRIN}} is a [[coniferous]] [[tree]] in the cypress family, [[Cupressaceae]], which is [[native plant|native]] to eastern Canada and much of the north-central and northeastern United States.<ref name=GRIN>{{GRIN|id=36584|name=Thuja occidentalis}}</ref><ref name=GD /> It is widely cultivated as an ornamental plant. It is not to be confused with ''[[Juniperus virginiana]]'' (eastern red cedar).

== Common names ==
Its additional common names include '''swamp cedar''',<ref name=GRIN /> '''American arborvitae''',<ref name=GD>{{Gymnosperm Database |family=Cupressaceae |genus=Thuja |species=occidentalis}}</ref> and '''eastern arborvitae'''.<ref name=GD /> The name arborvitae is particularly used in the [[horticulture|horticultural]] trade in the United States; it is [[Latin]] for 'tree of life' due to the supposed medicinal properties of the sap, bark, and twigs.<ref name="acs">''Thuja'', American Cancer Society, last revised 6/19/2007. [http://www.cancer.org/docroot/ETO/content/ETO_5_3X_Thuja.asp available online]</ref> It is sometimes called white-cedar (hyphenated) or whitecedar (one word){{r|GD}} to distinguish it from ''[[Cedrus]]'', the [[List of plants known as cedar#Family Pinaceae|true cedars]].{{r|cc}}

==Description==
Unlike the closely related [[Thuja plicata|western red cedar]] (''Thuja plicata''), northern white cedar is only a small or medium-sized tree, growing to a height of {{convert|15|m|ft|abbr=on}} tall with a {{Convert|0.9|m|ft|abbr=on}} trunk diameter, exceptionally to {{Convert|38|m|ft}} tall and {{Convert|1.8|m|ft}} diameter.<ref name="FNA">{{eFloras|1|200005456|Thuja occidentalis |family=Cupressaceae |first=Kenton L. |last=Chambers |access-date=24 September 2016}}</ref> The tree is often stunted or prostrate in less favorable locations. The [[bark (botany)|bark]] is red-brown, furrowed and peels in narrow, longitudinal strips.
Northern white cedar has fan-like branches and scaly leaves. The [[foliage]] forms in flat sprays with scale-like [[leaf|leaves]] {{Convert|3|-|5|mm|in|frac=16}} long.

The [[seed cone]]s are slender, yellow-green, ripening to brown, {{Convert|9|-|14|mm|in|frac=16}} long and {{Convert|4|-|5|mm|in|frac=32}} broad,{{citation needed|reason=breadth is not described by Flora of North America|date=September 2016}} with six to eight overlapping scales. They contain about eight seeds each.<ref name="FNA" /> The branches may take root if the tree falls.<ref name="GD" />

==Taxonomy==
The species was first described by [[Carl Linnaeus]] in 1753. Over 30 synonyms are listed in [[Kew]]'s [[Plants of the World Online]] database.{{r|powo}}

==Distribution==
Northern white cedar is [[species distribution|native]] to an area in the southern part of eastern Canada and the adjacent part of the northern United States. It extends from southeastern Manitoba east throughout the Great Lakes region and into [[Ontario]], [[Québec]], [[New York (state)|New York]], [[Vermont]], [[New Hampshire]], [[Maine]], [[Prince Edward Island]], [[New Brunswick]], and [[Nova Scotia]]. Isolated populations occur in west-central Manitoba, and to the south in [[Massachusetts]], [[Connecticut]], [[Ohio]], and [[Illinois]] and in the [[Appalachian Mountains]] of [[Kentucky]], [[Tennessee]], [[North Carolina]], [[Pennsylvania]], [[Maryland]], [[Virginia]], and [[West Virginia]].<ref name="GD" /> In Canada, its range reaches the [[Arctic treeline]] and the southern tip of [[Hudson Bay]]. It grows mainly in places with cooler summers, with a typical temperature of {{convert|16|to|22|C|F}} in July, and a shorter growing season, from 90 to 180 days.<ref name="silvics" />

==Ecology==
[[File:Superior Hiking Trail boardwalk.jpg|thumb|A swamp along the [[Superior Hiking Trail]] in November with a smattering of evergreen white cedars (left) and other trees and shrubs]]

Northern white cedar grows naturally in wet forests, being particularly abundant in [[coniferous swamp]]s, where other larger and faster-growing trees cannot compete successfully. It also occurs on other sites with reduced tree competition, such as [[cliffs]]. Although not currently listed as endangered, wild white cedar populations are threatened in many areas by high [[deer]] numbers; deer find the soft evergreen foliage a very attractive winter food and strip it rapidly. The largest known specimen is {{convert|34|m|ft|abbr=on}} tall and {{convert|175|cm|in|abbr=on}} diameter, on [[South Manitou Island]] within [[Leelanau County, Michigan]].{{citation needed|date=October 2020}}
Northern white cedars can be  very long-lived trees in certain conditions, with notably old specimens growing on cliffs where they are inaccessible to deer and [[wildfire]]. As of 2008, the oldest known living specimen was 1,141 years old,<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.ldeo.columbia.edu/~adk/oldlisteast/Spp/THOC.html |title=Eastern OLDLIST. ''Thuja occidentalis'' |year=2008 |publisher=Rocky Mountain Tree-Ring Research, Inc. & Eastern Kentucky University |access-date=15 January 2021}}</ref> but a dead specimen with 1,653 growth rings has been found.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.rmtrr.org/oldlist.htm |year=2020 |access-date=15 January 2021 |title=Eastern OLDLIST a database of ancient trees and their ages |publisher=Rocky Mountain Tree-Ring Research, Inc. & Eastern Kentucky University}}</ref> Despite their age, these very old trees are small and stunted due to the difficult growing conditions. These individuals' long lifespans have been attributed to their slow growth and their ability to survive when different sections of the tree are damaged or killed.<ref name="Larson2001">{{cite journal|last1=Larson|first1=D.W.|title=The paradox of great longevity in a short-lived tree species|journal=Experimental Gerontology|volume=36|issue=4–6|year=2001|pages=651–673|issn=0531-5565|doi=10.1016/S0531-5565(00)00233-3|pmid=11295506|s2cid=24297929}}</ref> The [[Witch Tree]], a ''T. occidentalis'' growing out of a cliff face on [[Lake Superior]] in [[Minnesota]], was described by the [[France|French]] explorer [[Pierre Gaultier de Varennes, sieur de La Vérendrye|Sieur de la Verendrye]] as being a mature tree in 1731; it is still alive today.

[[File:Something out of nothing 2.jpg|thumb|upright|Old trees growing on a rock ledge in [[Potawatomi State Park]], [[Wisconsin]]]]
Specimens found growing on cliff faces in southern Ontario are the oldest trees in [[Nearctic realm#Eastern North America|Eastern North America]] and all of Canada, having achieved ages in excess of 1,653 years.<ref name="GD" /> 

[[Wild type]] eastern white cedar is rare in [[Nova Scotia]], which is situated in the eastern limit of the tree's natural [[Species range|range]]. Only 34 natural stands of the tree are known from the province.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Newell |first=Ruth |date= |title=Provincial (Nova Scotia) Status Report on Northern White Cedar Thuja occidentalis |url=https://novascotia.ca/natr/wildlife/biodiversity/pdf/statusreports/StatusReportEasternCedar.pdf |url-status=live}}</ref> Due to its rarity, eastern white cedar is listed as [[Vulnerable species|vulnerable]] under the ''Nova Scotia Endangered Species Act.''<ref>{{Cite web |title=Cedar Lake |url=https://nsnt.ca/blog/cedar-lake/ |access-date=2026-05-27 |website=Nova Scotia Nature Trust}}</ref> 

==Uses==
''Thuja occidentalis'' is commercially used for rustic fencing and posts, lumber, poles, shingles, and in the construction of [[log cabin]]s.<ref name="silvics" /> It is the preferred wood for the structural elements, such as ribs and planking, of [[birchbark]] [[canoe]]s and the planking of wooden [[canoe]]s.<ref name="usda" />

The essential oil within the plant has been used for [[cleanser]]s, [[disinfectant]]s, hair preparations, [[insecticide]]s, [[liniment]], room sprays, and soft soaps. The Ojibwa reportedly made a soup from the inner bark of the soft twigs. Others have used the twigs to make teas to relieve [[constipation]] and [[headache]].<ref name="usda">{{cite web|url=https://plants.usda.gov/plantguide/pdf/cs_thoc2.pdf|title=USDA/NRCS Plant Guide: Northern White Cedar, ''Thuja occidentalis'' L.|publisher=[[United States Department of Agriculture]]|access-date=2008-02-15}}</ref>

Eastern white cedar – [[#Cultivation|as arborvitae]] – is a popular [[ornamental plant]] used in both residential and commercial landscapes.

''Thuja occidentalis'' has important uses in traditional [[Ojibwe people|Ojibwe]] culture. Honoured with the name '''Nookomis Giizhik''' (Grandmother Cedar), the tree is the subject of sacred legends and is considered a gift to humanity for its myriad of uses, among them crafts, construction, and medicine.<ref>Geniusz, Wendy Makoons (2009). ''Our Knowledge is not Primitive''. Syracuse, NY: Syracuse University Press</ref> It is one of the four plants of the Ojibwe [[medicine wheel]], associated with the north. The foliage is rich in [[vitamin C]] and is believed to be the [[aneda|annedda]], which cured the [[scurvy]] of [[Jacques Cartier]] and his party in the winter of 1535–1536.<ref name="silvics">{{Silvics |volume=1 |genus=Thuja |species=occidentalis |first=William F. |last=Johnston}}</ref> Due to the presence of the neurotoxic compound [[thujone]], internal use can be harmful if used for prolonged periods or while pregnant.{{citation needed|date=October 2020}}

==Cultivation==
[[File:Poland. Warsaw. Powsin. Botanical Garden 097.jpg|thumb|A grove of a columnar ornamental variety in [[Powsin Botanical Garden]], [[Warsaw, Poland]]]]
''T. occidentalis'' is widely used as an [[ornamental tree]], particularly for screens and [[Hedge (gardening)|hedges]], in gardens, parks, and cemeteries. Over 300 [[cultivar]]s exist, showing great variation in colour, shape, and size, with some of the more common ones being 'Degroot's Spire', 'Ellwangeriana', 'Hetz Wintergreen', 'Lutea', 'Rheingold', 'Smaragd' (or 'Emerald Green'), 'Techny', and 'Wareana'. It was introduced into [[Europe]] as early as 1540.{{citation needed|date=October 2020}}

These cultivars have gained the [[Royal Horticultural Society]]'s [[Award of Garden Merit]]:
*'Danica'<ref>{{cite web|title=RHS Plant Selector – ''Thuja occidentalis'' 'Danica'|url=https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/68725/Thuja-occidentalis-Danica/Details | publisher = RHS | access-date = 5 March 2021}}</ref>
*'Golden Tuffet'<ref>{{cite web | url = https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/220110/Thuja-occidentalis-Golden-Tuffet/Details | title = ''Thuja occidentalis'' 'Golden Tuffet' | publisher = RHS | access-date = 5 March 2021}}</ref>
*'Holmstrup'<ref>{{cite web|title=RHS Plant Selector – ''Thuja occidentalis'' 'Holmstrup'|url=https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/77166/Thuja-occidentalis-Holmstrup/Details | publisher = RHS | access-date = 5 March 2021}}</ref>
*'Rheingold'<ref>{{cite web|title=RHS Plant Selector – ''Thuja occidentalis'' 'Rheingold'|url=https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/91497/Thuja-occidentalis-Rheingold/Details | publisher = RHS | access-date = 5 March 2021}}</ref>
*'Smaragd'<ref>{{cite web|title=RHS Plant Selector – ''Thuja occidentalis'' 'Smaragd'|url=https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/75683/Thuja-occidentalis-Smaragd/Details | publisher = RHS | access-date = 5 March 2021}}</ref>
